soil-class-039.title: What a vineyard asks of its soil
soil-class-039.text: The best vineyard soil is thin. Vineyard soils are the soils in which grapevines grow, and their make-up is one of the most important considerations in planting a vineyard. Soil anchors the vine's roots and governs drainage and the minerals and nutrients the vine receives. The ideal is thin topsoil and subsoil that hold enough water yet drain well, so roots are not waterlogged. Soil that stores or reflects heat also affects ripening. Growers name soils by rock or texture. Limestone-based Kimmeridgian soil is the principal type of the Loire Valley, Champagne and Burgundy. Sandy soils drain well but hold water poorly, and the phylloxera louse does not thrive in them.

soil-found-101.title: Udic soils: moist enough, most years
soil-found-101.text: In humid climates, water moves down through the soil at some time in most years. The udic moisture regime belongs to such climates, where stored moisture plus rainfall roughly equals or exceeds evapotranspiration, the water lost from soil and plants to the air. In USDA soil taxonomy, udic soils are moist enough year-round in most years to meet plant needs. Drier soils fall into the {{ref:soil-class-041}} regime, between udic and aridic. Suborders with a udic regime include udalfs, part of {{ref:soil-class-090}}; udepts, part of {{ref:soil-class-100}}; and udolls, part of {{ref:soil-class-101}}.

soil-class-036.title: AASHTO groups: rating the soil beneath a road
soil-class-036.text: One sieve, with openings of 0.075 mm, splits road soils into two camps. The AASHTO Soil Classification System is an American highway-engineering system for soils and soil–aggregate mixtures used in road construction. Hogentogler and Terzaghi first developed it in 1929, and it has been revised several times since. Soils with 35% or less passing the 0.075 mm (No. 200) sieve are granular materials; those with more are silt–clay materials. Groups run from A-1 to A-7. They are set by sieve results and by the liquid limit and plasticity index of the fraction passing 0.425 mm (No. 40). As road subgrade, granular materials rate excellent to good, and silt–clay materials fair to poor.

soil-class-018.title: Naming a soil the WRB way, one qualifier at a time
soil-class-018.text: A WRB soil name can read like a short description. The WRB builds it in two steps: key the soil out to a Reference Soil Group, then add every qualifier that applies. The key asks, in a fixed sequence, whether given diagnostics occur in given depth ranges, plus traits such as clay content. The soil goes to the first group whose criteria it meets. Principal qualifiers precede the group name, the highest-ranked closest to it, and Haplic is used if none applies. Supplementary qualifiers follow in brackets. Specifiers such as Epi-, for 0 to 50 cm, and Endo-, for below 50 cm, turn qualifiers into depth-related subqualifiers such as Epiarenic. In the worked example, a loess soil with clay migration becomes an Amphialbic Endostagnic soil of the {{ref:soil-class-133}} group, with supplementary qualifiers such as Anosiltic, Endoloamic and Aric.

soil-class-019.title: How map scale sets the length of a WRB name
soil-class-019.text: A map of soils has room for only so many words. The WRB's rules for naming map units make the number of qualifiers depend on the map's scale. Three scale levels use the Reference Soil Group alone, the group plus its first applying principal qualifier, or the group plus the first two. Matching these levels to actual map scales is difficult, because the choice depends on how uniform the landscape is. Each map unit names an association of soils. Dominant soils cover at least 50%, codominant soils 25 to 50% and associated soils 5 to 25%; smaller shares are ignored. Only the third and later editions can build map legends; the second edition could only name soils.

soil-class-045.title: The argillic horizon, where washed-down clay collects
soil-class-045.text: In 44% of U.S. soil series, a 2014 study by James Bockheim found a clay-enriched layer below the surface. That layer is the argillic horizon, the USDA soil taxonomy term for a subsurface horizon enriched in clay. Clay builds up mainly by illuviation, the downward washing of existing clay, while some forms in place. To qualify, the horizon needs at least 1.2 times the clay of any overlying eluvial horizon. It usually shows clay films or bridges visible by eye or hand lens. It is a diagnostic horizon used to define higher categories. The orders in {{ref:soil-class-090}} and {{ref:soil-class-104}} require it, those in {{ref:soil-class-098}} and {{ref:soil-class-094}} never have it, and other orders vary. It is the starting point for kandic horizons, dominated by low-CEC 1:1 clays, and for natric horizons, rich in exchangeable sodium. Fragipans commonly form within it. The WRB equivalent is the argic horizon, from the same Latin root argilla; it needs at least 8% clay and a texture class other than sand. Buried paleo-argillic horizons, as in the Wounded Moose paleosol of the Yukon, show that the climate was once hot and wet enough to form them.

soil-class-040.title: Rankers: a thin topsoil straight on rock
soil-class-040.text: Some soils are little more than a topsoil laid directly on unaltered rock. A ranker is a soil developed over non-calcareous material, usually rock. It is often called an A/C soil, because its topsoil, the A horizon, sits directly on unaltered parent material, the C horizon. Some classifications group it as lithomorphic, together with the {{ref:soil-class-050}}, the similar soil over calcareous material. In the 1974 FAO legend, thin soils on acid rock were called Rankers. The {{ref:soil-class-034}} keeps rankers as a type of weakly developed soil, matched to the WRB's {{ref:soil-class-139}} group and to USDA Udorthents and Udifolists.

soil-class-041.title: Ustic soils: water, but not always enough
soil-class-041.text: In Brazil's Cerrado, a long dry season gives farmers a wide harvest window, and they harvest grain at a leisurely pace. That dry season marks the ustic regime, in which water is present but limited at times when conditions suit plant growth. It lies between aridic and udic. The name comes from Latin ustus, 'burnt', and the regime is common in semi-arid and sub-humid climates. Averaged over the year, stored moisture plus rainfall is less than the water lost by evapotranspiration. Ustic soils suit drought-tolerant crops. Maize there generally needs supplemental watering, which udic soils do not require.

soil-class-034.title: Poland's soil system and its three-part description
soil-class-034.text: Poland describes every soil three ways at once. The Polish Soil Classification is the system used to describe, classify and organize knowledge about the country's soils. Each soil gets a type, from its genesis and diagnostic horizons; a kind, the geological origin of the bedrock; and a texture class. The type is the basic unit, and types are grouped into orders by the presence or absence of diagnostic horizons and properties. The {{ref:soil-hist-057}} published editions in 1956, 1959, 1974, 1989, 2011 and 2019. Early ones followed Dokuchaev's natural criteria; the 2011 edition defined diagnostic horizons, materials and properties quantitatively. It borrows much from USDA soil taxonomy (1999) and the WRB (2006) and gives equivalents. Its rusty soils, sandy soils with rusty horizons, match WRB Arenosols and the U.S. {{ref:soil-class-108}} soils.

soil-class-043.title: Miami, Indiana's state soil on glacial till
soil-class-043.text: Some 794,994 acres (3,217 km2) of Indiana are mapped as one soil series, the Miami. It belongs to the Wisconsin Till Plains and is Indiana's state soil. It formed under native hardwood forest, in up to 18 inches (46 cm) of loess or silty material over calcareous loamy till. The fertile, gently sloping soils grow corn, soybeans and winter wheat, and they help rank the state in farm output. USDA soil taxonomy classifies it as fine-loamy, mixed, active, mesic Oxyaquic Hapludalfs, a member of the order in {{ref:soil-class-090}}. It is an old series: by 1906 it already held 16 soil types from glaciated regions.

soil-class-042.title: Pedalfers, the iron-and-aluminum soils of 1938
soil-class-042.text: At the top of Marbut's classification stood two camps: carbonate-rich pedocals and pedalfers. In the 1938 U.S. system, pedalfers were a major group of soils rich in aluminum and iron. In them, sesquioxides increase relative to silica as the soil forms. Pedalfers were a subdivision of the zonal order. They began at about the udic border, and lateritic soils were one of their three subdivisions. The term is no longer used in U.S. soil classification, but it survives in college geology texts. Its 'alf' lives on in the name of the order in {{ref:soil-class-090}}.

soil-class-032.title: Brunisolic soils, Canada's in-between order
soil-class-032.text: Almost 790,000 square kilometers of Canada, 8.6% of the country, is covered by soils that fit no other order. These are Brunisolic soils: soils with developed B horizons that meet the requirements of none of the other orders. They occur in all regions south of the permafrost zone. Many have brownish B horizons, without the clay build-up of {{ref:soil-class-031}} soils or the amorphous material of {{ref:soil-class-027}} soils. Some evolve into one or the other. Four great groups follow the A horizon and acidity. Melanic Brunisols have an Ah at least 10 cm thick and pH above 5.5, and Sombric Brunisols a thick Ah below pH 5.5. Eutric and Dystric Brunisols lack a thick Ah.

soil-class-025.title: Canada's Organic soils beneath bogs and fens
soil-class-025.text: Swamps, bogs and fens sit on soils made mostly of organic matter. Canada's Organic order holds such soils, with over 30% organic matter by weight in the upper half meter and no permafrost near the surface. Most are built from plants of waterlogged ground, though some come from lake deposits or from forest litter on rainy, rocky slopes. Organic soils cover almost 374,000 square kilometers, 4.1% of Canada, with large areas in Manitoba, Ontario and northern Alberta. Four great groups follow decomposition. Fibrisols are little decomposed, with over 40% fiber, mostly from Sphagnum. Two more have 10–40% fiber or up to 10%, and the last holds thick forest-litter soils over rock.

soil-class-030.title: Chernozemic soils of Canada's southern grasslands
soil-class-030.text: Decaying grass roots darken the topsoil across the grassy southern Interior Plains of Canada. These are Chernozemic soils, the Canadian order of grassland soils whose A horizon is darkened by organic matter. The A horizon is neutral to slightly acid and rich in bases such as calcium. The C horizon usually holds lime and may hold gypsum. With mean annual soil temperatures above 0 °C, these soils cover more than 4% of Canada. Four great groups follow surface color and dryness: Brown soils in the driest areas, Dark Brown soils, thick-topped Black soils under tall grass, and transitional Dark Gray soils.

soil-class-024.title: Cryosolic soils, frozen beneath 40% of Canada
soil-class-024.text: About 40% of Canada sits on soils with permafrost close below the surface. The Cryosolic order holds soils with permafrost within 1 meter of the surface, or 2 meters if strongly churned by frost. They cover about 3,672,000 square kilometers and dominate much of Yukon, the Northwest Territories and Nunavut. Because permafrost blocks roots and water, the seasonally thawed {{ref:soil-env-146}} above it can turn saturated and semifluid in spring. Disturbing the boreal forest or tundra cover melts ground ice. The thawing soil can then slide and settle, disrupting roads, pipelines and buildings. The order was defined in 1973 after surveys in the Mackenzie Valley. Its three great groups are Turbic Cryosols, mixed by cryoturbation; Static Cryosols, on sandy or gravelly material; and Organic Cryosols, rich in plant remains.

soil-class-028.title: Gleysolic soils: gray ground where water lingers
soil-class-028.text: Flood a soil warmer than about 5 °C, and microbes use up its oxygen within days. Nitrate and ferric oxide are then reduced, and losing ferric oxide turns the soil gray. When it dries, reoxidized iron forms yellow-brown mottles. Poor drainage and a drab gray color therefore identify the Gleysolic order: Canadian soils periodically or permanently saturated with water and depleted of oxygen. They cover about 117,000 square kilometers, 1.3% of Canada, in depressions and level areas of subhumid and humid climates. Three great groups are defined: Humic Gleysols, with a dark organic A horizon; plain Gleysols, without one; and Luvic Gleysols, with a clay-enriched B horizon.

soil-class-031.title: Luvisolic soils, where clay moves down under forest
soil-class-031.text: Under forest, clay can leave one layer of a soil and settle in the next. The Luvisolic order holds Canadian soils with a leached Ae horizon above a Bt horizon, where the washed-down clay has been deposited. They typically form under forest, in subhumid to humid climates where the parent material holds appreciable clay. In saline or calcareous material, salts and carbonates leach out before the clay moves. Luvisolic soils cover about 809,000 square kilometers, 8.8% of Canada, largely in the central to northern Interior Plains. Two great groups split by soil temperature. Gray Brown Luvisols, at 8 °C or more, lie in the Great Lakes–St Lawrence Lowlands; Gray Luvisols belong to the boreal Interior Plains.

soil-class-027.title: Podzolic soils under Canada's conifers
soil-class-027.text: Organic acids from forest litter can free iron and aluminum and carry them down through a soil. The result is the Podzolic order: acid soils whose B horizon accumulates amorphous humified organic matter bound to aluminum and iron. These soils form mostly in sandy materials under forest or shrubs in cold, humid climates. Percolating water leaches bases. The metal–organic complexes become insoluble and settle in the B horizon once the metals reach a critical proportion. Podzolic soils occupy 14.3% of Canada, in the Appalachian Uplands, the Canadian Shield and British Columbia, usually under coniferous forest. Great groups follow the B horizon. Humic Podzols are low in iron, Ferro-Humic Podzols hold at least 5% organic carbon, and Humo-Ferric Podzols, the commonest, hold less than 5%.

soil-class-033.title: Regosolic soils, too young for layers
soil-class-033.text: Some soils still look much like the material they came from. The Regosolic order holds Canada's weakly developed soils, whose properties are essentially those of their parent material. They support plants but have not been stable long enough to develop well-differentiated horizons. The name joins Greek rhēgos, 'blanket', with Latin solum, 'soil'. These soils cover about 0.8% of Canada. Two great groups are defined: one made essentially of C horizons, and a humic one with an Ah horizon at least 10 cm thick.

soil-class-029.title: Solonetzic soils, rock-hard when dry, sticky when wet
soil-class-029.text: Some Canadian subsoils are very hard when dry and swell into a sticky, compact mass when wet. Sodium is the reason. Its ions make the clay disperse and swell on wetting, closing large pores and stopping water flow. Soils with such a B horizon form the Solonetzic order, which usually develops in saline parent materials of semiarid and subhumid regions. It covers almost 73,000 square kilometers, 0.7% of Canada, mostly in southern Alberta. As leaching moves salts and sodium downward, the soil develops from saline parent material through two sodium-rich stages to a final, leached stage called Solod. Resalinization can reverse the sequence.

soil-class-026.title: Vertisolic soils, churned by their own clay
soil-class-026.text: Some clay soils turn themselves over. In the Vertisolic order, clay-rich soils shrink and swell markedly as they dry and wet. The movement cuts shiny slickensides in the subsoil, mixes former surface material downward, and prevents or scrambles subsurface horizons. These soils form mainly in clayey materials of the semiarid to subhumid Interior Plains and cover less than 1% of Canada. The order was recognized in the 1990s, after studies of Great Plains pedons. Its two great groups are told apart by the darkness of the A horizon, the darker one being humic.

soil-class-044.title: Anthroposols, soils that people built or remade
soil-class-044.text: An Anthroposol is a soil profoundly modified or constructed by people, with one or more natural horizons altered, removed or replaced. Such soils occur on industrial, commercial, urban and resource-extraction sites, and along transport, fuel and power corridors. Classification systems long left them out, because criteria built for natural soils often do not apply. A proposed Canadian order requires a disturbed D horizon at least 10 cm thick, or removed natural horizons. Its great groups would be set by artefacts or organic carbon, and ordinary plowing does not qualify. The WRB splits such soils into two groups: long-cultivated {{ref:soil-class-120}} soils and {{ref:soil-class-145}} soils holding industrial products and artefacts. Australia's system also has an Anthroposol order.

soil-found-070.title: Kurosols: a light topsoil over acid clay
soil-found-070.text: In eastern and southern Australia, many soils change abruptly a short way down. Kurosols are one of the fifteen orders of the Australian Soil Classification: soils with a sharp texture contrast between a lighter surface and a strongly acidic, clay-rich subsoil. The upper B horizon sets them apart from other texture-contrast orders. It is strongly acidic in kurosols, sodic in sodosols, and neither in chromosols. That acidic subsoil generally has a pH below 5.5 measured in water. Kurosols are widespread in higher-rainfall, strongly leached and weathered landscapes. The dense clay and the acidity can restrict roots and water and cause aluminum and manganese toxicity. Lime corrects surface acidity, but deep acidity is hard to fix.

soil-class-035.title: France's Référentiel pédologique
soil-class-035.text: France names its soils with words like Colluviosol, Fluviosol and Reductisol. These belong to the Référentiel pédologique, the French soil reference system, a natural classification based on presumed soil genesis. Like the WRB, it has two hierarchical levels. Versions appeared in 1992, 1995 and 2008. Its reference soil types, relevant to European soils, include Brunisol, Calcarisol, Colluviosol, Fluviosol, Podzosol and Reductisol, refined by terms such as humic or typic.

soil-class-047.title: Greyzem, the grey earth of the FAO system
soil-class-047.text: A Greyzem's name is half English, half Russian: 'grey' plus zemlja, 'earth'. This soil group of the FAO soil classification is named for the uncoated silt and quartz grains in its organic-rich layers. It forms in decalcified loose deposits such as wind-blown, river and lake sediments and glacial till. With {{ref:soil-class-123}}, {{ref:soil-class-130}} and {{ref:soil-class-135}} soils, it forms a set of steppe and prairie soils with a mollic horizon, where organic matter accumulates faster than leaching removes it. One of the original 26 FAO groups, it remained among the 28 of the 1988 revision, with two units: gleyic and haplic greyzems. It correlates most closely with the Dark Gray great group of Canada's Chernozemic order, and with Albolls and Boralfic Boroll subgroups in USDA soil taxonomy.

soil-class-046.title: The Handbook of Australian Soils
soil-class-046.text: Before today's system, Australians classified their soils with a handbook. The Handbook of Australian Soils, first published in 1968, was an earlier system developed for the continent's soils. It built on the great soil group classification that J. A. Prescott published in 1931. The Australian Soil Classification has since superseded it, as it did the 1960 Factual Key.

soil-class-015.title: Zonal soils, shaped by regional climate
soil-class-015.text: In the 1938 U.S. system, a zonal soil was one whose character reflects the regional climate and vegetation. Both pedocals and pedalfers were subdivisions of this order. The idea long shaped how soils were explained. Fertile, carbon-rich dark soils of North America and Eurasia were long read as zonal soils of dry continental climates under steppe or prairie. Only later was past human activity recognized as a driver of them.

soil-class-014.title: Azonal soils, never given time to mature
soil-class-014.text: On Himalayan slopes, fine weathered material slides downhill so constantly that soil has no time to form. Such places hold azonal soils: immature soils that never develop because their material keeps sliding downslope or is buried by fresh deposits. River flood plains are the other classic case. New alluvium arrives every year, so the soils stay immature even though the farmland is fertile. The label is also given to the {{ref:soil-class-127}} group, found in nearly all climates. Canada's system calls Anthroposols azonal soils, highly modified or built by people.

soil-class-013.title: Intrazonal soils, ruled by local conditions
soil-class-013.text: Limestone or waterlogged ground can outweigh the regional climate in shaping a soil. Intrazonal soils are those whose profiles reflect a dominant local factor of relief or parent material more than the zonal effects of climate and vegetation. Calcimorphic soils develop from limestone. They include the thin {{ref:soil-class-050}}, with limited available water, and the deep red {{ref:soil-class-051}} of wetter climates. Hydromorphic soils form in waterlogged ground. In gley soils, waterlogged, airless pores reduce iron and turn the soil grey-blue with red flecks. In soils of {{ref:soil-class-070}}, plant remains never fully break down. Halomorphic soils form through salinization.

reviews.classification-systems: Every system in this chapter answers one question differently: which traits should decide a soil's name? Engineering schemes sort soils by behavior and strength, natural systems by properties and genesis, and U.S. soil mapping runs both side by side. The 1938 U.S. system keyed soils to climate, vegetation and local factors; its replacement, USDA soil taxonomy, uses measurable properties across six levels, down to more than 14,000 series. Canada, Australia, Poland and France built national systems with orders that fit their own land, from Cryosolic soils over about 40% of Canada to Australia's acid Kurosols. Above them all, the FAO legend gave way in 1998 to the WRB, whose 32 Reference Soil Groups and their qualifiers let a soil carry the same name everywhere.
